newsitem.title: UK: EMS/Mark sheds gains in late Europe, lira up.
newsitem.headline: EMS/Mark sheds gains in late Europe, lira up.

text.p: The lira slid quite dramatically after news that a compromise plan that would allow Italy to join in with European monetary union (EMU) after 1999 was being considered, although the news came as little surprise in financial markets.
"I'm not surprised in the least," said David Brown, chief economist at Bear Stearns. "This is just confirmation of what's been lurking in the back of the market's subconscious for a long while."
Mark/lira was at 992.00 versus 986.00 on Tuesday.
The lira has been riding high on EMU expectations for some time, but it was an accident waiting to happen because markets tend to get over-optimistic and overshoot, analysts said.
"The Italian economy has been converging, but there has been an awful lot of premium in there because of EMU expectations," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
"If you delay and possibly, even postpone Italy's membership, it has to follow that some of that premium has to be wiped out."
The story first broke in the Financial Times newspaper, and the lira began to slide when early editions hit the streets around midnight U.K. time.
The Financial Times report quoted senior monetary officials, while later official comments confirming that a plan was being considered came from Brussels.
Judging from the first response from Italy -- which reiterated it would not consider late entry into EMU and knew nothing of such a plan -- the indications were the country had no say whatsoever.

These developments mean that Friday's EMU meeting in Bonn between Italian Prime Minister Ramano Prodi and Chancellor Helmut Kohl will be far from a cosy chat about the single currency, and some economists see potential for a full scale diplomatic row.
Later comments from a German source, saying that while officials may be discussing EMU scenarios politicians were not, livened up the debate further.
There was also an angry response from Prime Minister Prodi who said the reports of EMU delay for Italy were "false, unjustified and unfounded."

As the political row gathered pace, and with so much good news priced into the lira, there could be further problems ahead. "If there is less than ringing endorsement from Germany about Italy's quest for early EMU membership on Friday the market could get more upset this week," Bear Stearns Brown said.
The peseta and escudo showed little reaction to the news but today's developments on Italy raised a questionmark in the market about EMU implications for Spain and Portugal.
They have sparked the theory that even though Spain and Portugal may qualify for EMU on time the hard-core countries may decide to exclude them to preserve the hardness of the new euro.
"All this is about the dilution risks of Club-Med being included and effectively the hard-core EU want to keep the euro as hard as they can get it," Brown said.
"You can't extract good news out of this but this must raise the question whether Italy takes part in EMU at all."
Some see today's developments as confirmation that EMU will go ahead of time albeit without the peripheral Club-Med countries.

"The politicans have said it's going to start on time but the Bundesbank are saying pretty clearly that once it starts it is going to be as hard as possible," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International.
Phil Smith, London Forex desk +44-171-542-6284.
